items.title: James Moody interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998
items.q: When I joined Dizzy’s band in ‘46... Dave Burns, Miles was in the band...

ctx.x: Chi-chi — I think is thank you, isn’t it?

But you see what I’m saying though? And like if a kid sees something, and you show it to him, and he can do it slowly, and — oh, I see that. It’s simple. They call it the light bulb going on. And I always say this, like I’ve been kind of fortunate, because if I explain something to you this way and you don’t get it, I can explain it four, five, six different other ways, like I think I can, because I’ve been pretty fortunate I’ve been able to do that. Because I hate for someone to come to me for someone, and I’m…
That’s right. This is live. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

items.title: James Moody — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So I met Dizzy and Diz said to me and Dave Burns... 'come and try out for it.' So that's what we did when we were discharged -- I was discharged in 1946 and Dave was, too... And Dave Burns, trumpet.

ctx.x: Uh-huh. [affirmative] Yeah. So I went in 1943 and came out 1946, discharged. But, you know, it was different being -- just different being down South because there was a different mentality down there. Not only -- not only with so called Caucasians, but with the Negroes, too. It just did -- people thought differently, you know. There was a subservient attitude seen, you know. And I used to -- I used to be amazed, said, "Damn! I wonder why," you know, I'm looking at people and I'm saying, "Why are they supposed to…
